query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor (~2 atomic percent) aluminum modification to equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr will lead to the in situ formation of a continuous, adherent alumina (Al2O3) scale during high‐temperature air exposure, thereby improving its oxygen resistance while preserving its room- and high-temperature mechanical properties.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr that exhibits good ductility at room temperature and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C but suffers from inadequate oxygen resistance.
generation.intervention: Incorporate a ~2 at.% aluminum addition into the alloy composition during processing.
generation.conditions: Exposure to air at approximately 800 °C for a duration of 5 hours, under conditions similar to prior mechanical testing (strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹ at high temperature and standard tensile testing at room temperature).
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a continuous, protective alumina layer on the surface.
generation.mechanism: Due to its high affinity for oxygen, the minor aluminum addition preferentially oxidizes to form a slow-growing, dense alumina scale. This scale acts as a barrier to further oxygen ingress, slowing or preventing pesting without altering the dislocation mechanisms that underpin the alloy’s high ductility and yield strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy will show a markedly reduced oxygen uptake and pesting behavior during a 5-hour air exposure at 800 °C, while maintaining tensile ductility at room temperature and comparable high‐temperature yield strength relative to the untreated alloy.
generation.baseline: Untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, which under identical conditions exhibits significant oxygen-induced degradation (pesting) despite having good mechanical performance.
generation.boundary: The effect is anticipated for high-temperature conditions around 800 °C in an air environment over periods of up to 5 hours; mechanical loadings (both tensile tests at room temperature and high-temperature yield evaluations) remain within the ranges previously established for the undoped alloy.
generation.uncertainty: The optimum aluminum content and its uniform distribution must be validated to ensure that the protective alumina scale forms without detrimental effects on the alloy’s microstructure or mechanical performance. Interactions with the existing elements in the alloy during oxidation also introduce uncertainty.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloys: one set as the control and one modified with ~2 at.% aluminum. Process both via the same casting route. Expose specimens from each batch to air at 800 °C for 5 hours. After exposure, perform surface characterization (SEM/EDS, XRD) to assess oxide scale formation and measure mass gains. Follow up with tensile testing at room temperature and high-temperature (e.g., 1000 °C) yield tests to evaluate if the mechanical properties have been preserved.
measurements: Surface oxide scale thickness and phase identification via SEM/EDS and XRD
Mass gain per unit surface area indicating oxidation rate
Room-temperature tensile ductility and yield strength
High-temperature yield strength at established strain rates
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aluminum-doped alloy does not form a continuous or protective alumina scale (as evidenced by similar or higher mass gain and poorly adherent oxides), or if its post-exposure mechanical properties (ductility and yield strength) are significantly degraded compared to the control, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Question: Can high-entropy alloys be designed to simultaneously achieve high Snoek-type damping capacity, high mechanical strength, and high ductility at elevated temperatures?. System: Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi base HEA, (Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi)98O2 (O-2 HEA), and (Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi)98N2 (N-2 HEA). Processing: Arc-melting of pure metals (purity >99.9 wt%), TiN (99.9 wt%), and TiO2 (99.9 wt%) in a Ti-gettered high-purity argon atmosphere; remelted at least eight times; drop-cast into a water-cooled copper mold (10 mm × 10 mm × 60 mm). Test conditions: Damping measured via multifunction internal friction apparatus at 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, and 4.0 Hz, temperature range 300–1100 K, heating rate 2 K min⁻¹, max strain amplitude 2 × 10⁻⁴; Tensile tests at room temperature, strain rate 1 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹. Findings: The O-2 HEA achieved a peak damping capacity (tanδ_max) of 0.020 at 1.0 Hz, while the N-2 HEA reached 0.027 at 1.0 Hz.; The N-2 HEA exhibited a yield strength of 1362 MPa and elongation of ~11.9%, while the O-2 HEA showed 1138 MPa yield strength and ~20% elongation.; The peak damping temperature (T_p) for the HEAs was approximately 730–747 K at 1.0 Hz, roughly 100 K higher than traditional Snoe
